payload: Parody and satire differ by target: a parody imitates a specific existing work to mock or comment on that work itself and cannot exist without the original, while satire borrows a familiar style merely as a tool to make a broader point about systemic topics. Galaxy Quest (1999) is parody — it specifically sends up Star Trek's ensemble cast, its washed-up actors, and its episodic villain format — whereas Bowfinger (1999) is satire, targeting Hollywood's greed and blind ambition rather than any one film or director. Legally, parody gets more fair-use protection because it comments on the borrowed work, whereas satire (as in the 1997 Dr. Seuss 'The Cat NOT in the Hat' case using Seuss's style to talk about the O.J. Simpson trial) is less protected because it only leverages a work's popularity to draw attention.
notes: Fair use is weighed on four factors: (1) purpose/character of the use (courts favor transformative, educational, or news use); (2) nature of the copyrighted work (creative works get more protection than factual); (3) amount and substantiality used; (4) effect on the potential market for the original.

In Dr. Seuss Enterprises v. Penguin Books, the Ninth Circuit ruled 'The Cat NOT in the Hat' infringed because it was satire (borrowing Seuss's style for attention) not parody (commenting on Seuss's work), so it lost fair-use protection and was never fully published.

The everyday test the creator lands on: ask 'what is the target?' — parody is a 'love letter' aimed at the original text (you can't make Galaxy Quest without loving Star Trek); satire keeps distance from its target.

Framing example: Kyle Gordon's song/video 'Mr. Jambo' is both — parodying Paul Simon's Graceland sound while satirizing white artists who mine existing (e.g., South African) musical traditions. From the channel 'Essays on Frame.'
